reader_questions.q: What makes France’s debt situation a crisis now, rather than simply a high level of government borrowing?
How large are France’s debt, annual deficit and interest payments relative to its economy, its revenues and comparable countries?
reader_questions.where: The opening snapshot gives revenue, spending and the deficit; the final section gives debt of €3.6 trillion, or 119% of GDP. Interest payments, debt relative to revenue and international comparisons are missing.

reader_questions.q: What drove the debt build-up, and how much reflects persistent spending and tax choices versus economic shocks?
reader_questions.where: “Bigger bills, but not always a bigger share of the economy” and “The deficit also has a revenue side” discuss inflation, tax reductions and persistent deficits, but do not apportion the debt build-up between policy choices and shocks.

reader_questions.q: What changed, and when, to make lenders or policymakers more worried about France’s ability to manage its debt?
How do economic growth, borrowing costs and membership of the euro affect the risk that France’s debt becomes unmanageable?
reader_questions.where: “Repeated gaps accumulate into debt” notes that GDP growth changes the debt ratio. It does not explain the interaction between growth and borrowing costs or the role of euro membership.

reader_questions.q: What could realistically stabilise the debt, and what political or economic obstacles stand in the way?
Who bears the costs of the crisis and of the measures proposed to resolve it?

missed_findings: The debt chart shows a 16.7-percentage-point increase in 2020, a 5.4-point decline through 2023 and a 9.5-point rebound by June 2026, a useful chronology that the story never explains.
The 2025 deficit remained 2.7 percentage points of GDP above its 2019 level despite its latest improvement, sharpening the question of why the pandemic-era deterioration has not fully unwound.

The reported total and pre-interest deficits suggest interest payments of roughly 2.1% of GDP in 2025, but the Eurostat and IMF definitions and vintages would need reconciliation before publishing that calculation.
There is no evidence of market stress or a dated policy trigger—such as borrowing spreads, refinancing pressure or a documented loss of fiscal credibility—to establish why this is a crisis now.
Comparable-country debt and interest burdens, debt-stabilisation scenarios and the euro’s institutional role are missing, leaving the reader unable to judge whether France’s debt is manageable.
The spending breakdown identifies beneficiaries but supplies no proposed adjustment, political constraints or distributional evidence showing who would bear its costs.

charts.shows: Government spent €153 billion more than it collected in 2025, with receipts covering about €91 of every €100 spent.
Social protection and health together accounted for 57.1% of government spending in 2024.
Old age accounts for more than half of social protection spending and nearly a quarter of all public spending.
Social protection grew in euros but fell relative to GDP between 2014 and 2024; the chart also shows longer-run health and protection trends and nine subgroup comparisons.
charts.fix: Remove the subgroup panel so the figure concentrates on the nominal-growth-versus-GDP-share finding rather than combining several comparisons.

charts.shows: Spending exceeded revenue throughout 1995–2025, and falling revenue relative to GDP outweighed falling spending between 2022 and 2024.
charts.fix: Mark the 2022 and 2024 observations directly on the lines so the recent deterioration is visible in the plot, rather than only in its footnote.

charts.shows: The deficit narrowed to 5.1% of GDP in 2025 but remained above its pre-pandemic level.
Debt rose substantially over the long run, fell relative to GDP after 2020 and then climbed to 119% by June 2026.
charts.fix: Annotate the post-2023 increase of 9.5 percentage points to bring the latest deterioration into focus.

top_change: Rebuild the story around why a persistent fiscal deficit has become a crisis now, using dated evidence of financing or political stress and explaining the growth, interest-cost and policy conditions needed to stabilise debt; compress the spending taxonomy to make room.

lessons.rule: Keep the commissioned question as the organising argument, even when the available data supports an appealing adjacent story.
lessons.evidence: The commission asks why France has a debt crisis; the title and opening instead ask where public money goes.

lessons.rule: Distinguish evidence of a large debt burden from evidence of an immediate crisis.
lessons.evidence: The story establishes persistent deficits and debt of 119% of GDP but presents no lender behaviour, refinancing pressure or political trigger.

lessons.rule: Use spending composition to explain budget size, and separate evidence to explain changes in deficits and debt.
lessons.evidence: The story correctly observes that social protection’s large share cannot explain a deficit widening while spending falls relative to GDP.

lessons.rule: Give each chart one main comparison and place the decisive evidence in the plotted area.
lessons.evidence: The evolution figure combines aggregate history, subgroup changes and nominal growth, while the revenue chart relegates its key recent comparison to a footnote.

lessons.rule: Explain debt sustainability through mechanisms and feasible choices, including who bears their costs.
lessons.evidence: The final paragraph distinguishes stocks from flows but stops before borrowing costs, euro membership, stabilisation options or distributional consequences.

argument.why: There is a coherent argument about spending and revenues, but it answers a different question from why France has a debt crisis.

depth.why: Attributed explanations of revenue weakness and benefit indexation add depth, but the central crisis mechanism and sustainability comparison are absent.

charts.why: Charts are labelled and generally well matched to their comparisons, but the evolution figure carries several points and none establishes the crisis.

honesty.why: Sources, periods, units, revisions and nominal-versus-GDP distinctions are supplied; causal explanations are attributed and the limits on inference are explicit.

reader_questions.why: Four questions are unanswered and three only partly answered, including no explanation of why this is a crisis now.

prose.why: Mostly clear and concrete, but unexplained phrases such as “cycle-adjusted assessment” and extensive accounting distinctions consume space needed for the commissioned explanation.
